sections.title: Framing the infection history: patient, place, time and fever

blocks.text: Kumar frames every infection history around one question: **why has this patient, from this place, come now, with these symptoms?** That gives four headings to work through: the **patient** (age, sex, job, co-morbidity, immune status), the **place** (travel, previous residence, care homes or hospitals), the **time** course, and the **symptoms**. Kumar calls the history the single most important part of the diagnostic assessment. Davidson stresses that the **duration** of the complaint changes the differential: fever and cough for 2 days points to an acute respiratory infection, but the same pair for 2 months points to TB.

blocks.title: Fever symptoms: what each one tells you
rows: Davidson: core temperature **above 38.0°C**, actually recorded. It is driven by cytokines and acute phase proteins and has infective and non-infective causes
Feeling hot or sweaty is not proof. Axillary and ear readings are less accurate than oral or rectal ones
A fast rise in temperature, whatever the cause. Talley flags rigors as a red-flag question because shaking chills suggest **bacteraemia**
Kumar's list for shivers and rigors: bloodstream infection, malaria, influenza, endocarditis
Sweating from any cause is worse at night
Alcohol, anxiety, thyrotoxicosis, diabetes, acromegaly, lymphoma, a hot environment
Check that fever has been documented before you chase an infection

blocks.title: Time course clues
items: **Short, acute history** (days) favours acute pathogens. Example: 3 days of shivers, green sputum and pleuritic pain suggests pneumococcal pneumonia

**More than 2 weeks** suggests a chronic infection (TB, leishmaniasis, brucellosis, HIV) or a non-infective cause (autoimmune, malignant). Rigors with a history of 2 weeks or more should raise PUO causes
**Abrupt, severe onset** suggests a virulent organism and may justify empirical treatment before the diagnosis is known
**Characteristic patterns:** biphasic fever in dengue; Katayama fever followed later by haematuria in _Schistosoma haematobium_

**Incubation-period logic:** if symptoms began after the longest incubation period of an exposure, that exposure is an unlikely cause (e.g. ask about chickenpox or shingles contact in the previous **21 days** for a new vesicular rash). This does not apply to colonisers such as _Staph. aureus_

blocks.title: Symptom clusters that point to a site
rows: Headache, neck stiffness, photophobia + non-blanching rash
Sore ulcerated mouth + rash on hands and feet
Hand, foot and mouth disease (remember syphilis with palm/sole rashes)
Biliary infection, liver abscess, or pneumonia next to the diaphragm
Discitis, with or without epidural abscess
Septic arthritis (also consider gout and reactive arthritis)

blocks.title: Accompanying features (Davidson)
items: Severe headache with photophobia is typical of meningitis but also occurs in other infections
Delirium with fever is commoner at the extremes of age (young children, the elderly)
Myalgia occurs in viral infections such as influenza and in sepsis, including meningococcal sepsis
Shock can accompany severe infection and sepsis

blocks.text: Exam keyword patterns (quick-source): fever + constipation + rash + **relative bradycardia** = typhoid; fever + chills + sweats after a trip to Africa = malaria; sore throat + lymphadenopathy + a rash **after ampicillin** = infectious mononucleosis; fever + GI upset + tender hepatomegaly + basal crackles = amoebic liver abscess.

Apparently localising symptoms can mislead. Headache, breathlessness and diarrhoea occur in sepsis or malaria with no infection in the brain, lung or gut, and a basal pneumonia can present with abdominal pain. Vomiting or watery diarrhoea alone does not mean GI disease.
Not every fever is infective, and not every infection is febrile. Fever is often intermittent (so may be absent when you see the patient) and is less common in the elderly.

In sepsis, do not delay treatment to take a full history: take it after or during emergency management. Isolate first if a highly transmissible infection is possible, and get the history from a relative or friend if the patient is confused.

blocks.title: Medical, drug and contact history
rows: Define the host and how likely infection is; surgical or dental procedures that left prosthetic material; previous infections
Review microbiology from the **last 12 months** (e.g. MRSA colonisation, resistant organisms) to guide empirical antibiotics
Over-the-counter drugs, antimicrobials, immunosuppressants; drugs that interact with antimicrobials or can **cause fever**
PPIs and H2 blockers raise the risk of _Salmonella_ and _C. difficile_ (not norovirus, which is acid-insensitive); recent antimicrobials predict resistant organisms
A rash and anaphylaxis have very different implications for future prescribing
Age- and job-related vaccines; adherence to prophylaxis; family or household illness; sensitive enquiry about TB and HIV exposure
Recurrent boils in the patient and contacts suggest PVL-producing _Staph. aureus_

blocks.title: Exposure history: travel, work, leisure, animals, food, needles and sex
rows: Countries visited and where the patient has lived; full itinerary including stopovers; earlier trips; type of environment and length of stay
Childhood residence predicts BCG status; old trips matter for relapsing infections such as _P. vivax_
Unbottled water, local food or hotels; swimming; insects and animals; sick contacts; sex; drug use; injections, procedures or admissions abroad; vaccines; malaria prophylaxis
Hospital treatment abroad carries a risk of antibiotic-resistant bacteria
Anthrax in leather tannery workers; healthcare workers exposed to TB, chickenpox, rotavirus and needlestick blood-borne viruses; teachers to childhood infections
Water sports, unusual hobbies (caving, aquarium cleaning, air-conditioning repair)
Leptospirosis in canoeists and windsurfers; freshwater swimming also risks schistosomiasis in some regions
Dogs and hydatid disease; cats and toxoplasmosis or cat-scratch disease; sheep and Q fever (_Coxiella burnetii_); bats and rabies
Undercooked meat, shellfish, unpasteurised dairy, well water; **who else ate it**
Injecting drug use, blood products, tattoos, piercing

Blood-borne viruses (HIV-1, HBV, HCV); _Staph. aureus_ and group A strep infections; groin abscesses and pseudoaneurysms, psoas abscess, osteomyelitis, spinal infection, often **right-sided** endocarditis
Taken confidentially; often omitted or done badly
Heterosexual sex is the **commonest** route of HIV-1 transmission worldwide; sexual exposure is common in travellers

blocks.title: Host factors that shift the differential
items: **Age:** children and the very old are more susceptible to some infections
**Sex-specific diagnoses:** epididymo-orchitis or prostatitis in men; PID or tampon-related toxic shock in women
**Pregnancy:** more susceptible to malaria, HIV and listeriosis; at risk of severe disseminated HSV, hepatitis E, influenza, malaria and measles
**Alcohol excess:** spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (with ascites), invasive pneumococcal disease, TB
**Splenectomy:** capsulated bacteria (pneumococcus, _Haemophilus_, meningococcus)
**Recent influenza:** secondary group A strep or meningococcal infection
**Nursing-home residents:** hospital-type infections such as hospital-acquired pneumonia and _C. difficile_

**Net state of immunosuppression:** add up age, co-morbidity and drugs; the first **6 months** after solid organ transplant carry the highest risk; transplant or marrow disease opens the door to fungi, low-virulence viruses and non-tuberculous mycobacteria
**Second dengue infection** carries a higher risk of severe disease

blocks.text: Immunocompromised patients may have few localising symptoms or signs, may mount **no fever or neutrophilia**, and can deteriorate suddenly. Keep a high index of suspicion and investigate early.
Do not skip the sexual history because the patient seems low-risk: Davidson reminds you that most HIV-1 is acquired heterosexually, and Kumar notes the sexual history is the part most often omitted.

blocks.note: World map of where selected pathogens occur (P. falciparum malaria, typhoid, yellow fever, dengue/Zika, MERS, MDR-TB, CRE): use it to interpret a travel history

sections.title: Systematic examination of the febrile patient

blocks.text: Examine **every system** in a febrile patient, because the key sign is often small: splinter haemorrhages of endocarditis or the first few petechiae of meningococcal disease. Start with general observation: **temperature** (repeat it and review the chart for a pattern), sweating, weight loss, respiratory distress, conscious level, pallor and jaundice, and decide how ill the patient looks. Remove dressings and inspect every wound and device site.

blocks.title: Head-to-toe checklist (Davidson's clinical examination page)
rows: Clubbing, splinter haemorrhages, Janeway lesions (endocarditis), chronic liver disease stigmata, vasculitic lesions; arthropathy or Raynaud's suggests connective tissue disease
Rash, generalised erythema, injection track marks, surgical scars, central lines and cannula sites, tattoos; epitrochlear and axillary nodes
Conjunctival petechiae, painful red eye (uveitis), lost red reflex (endophthalmitis), Roth's spots (endocarditis), CMV retinitis, choroidal TB lesions
Lymphadenopathy, parotid swelling, abnormal eardrums, dental caries, tonsillar swelling or exudate, candidiasis
Tachycardia, hypotension, murmurs or prosthetic valve sounds, pericardial rub, consolidation, pleural or pericardial effusion
Hepatosplenomegaly, ascites, renal angle tenderness, local tenderness or guarding (e.g. left iliac fossa in diverticulitis), masses, surgical drains
Ulcers, discharge, testicular swelling or nodules, inguinal nodes, a tender prostate, rectal fluctuance
Hot, swollen, tender joints; focal spinal tenderness (epidural abscess, discitis); a draining sinus of chronic osteomyelitis
Neck stiffness, photophobia, delirium, focal signs

blocks.title: Rash patterns in infection
rows: Painful, indurated violaceous nodules on the shins
Erythema nodosum (often triggered by infection, but has non-infective causes too)
2–4 mm flat red spots that blanch, on upper abdomen and lower chest

blocks.title: Linking examination findings to a site (Kumar)
rows: Tonsillitis or a glandular fever syndrome (including HIV)
Diverticular abscess / appendix abscess (ovarian abscess in women on either side)
IV device with redness or pus

blocks.text: A red, hot, swollen limb is usually cellulitis, but think **necrotising fasciitis** when the pain is severe or out of proportion to what you see, the history progresses fast, or the appearance is 'odd'.
A new fever in a hospital inpatient means **remove the peripheral cannula and send the tip for culture**. Talley warns that peripheral cannulae cause sepsis and deaths in hospital.
Every rash on the infection list has non-infective look-alikes (drugs, SLE, erythema multiforme). Always include them in the differential.

blocks.note: Davidson's examination diagram of the febrile patient, with insets of splinter haemorrhages and Roth's spots (endocarditis), streptococcal tonsillitis, CXR consolidation and mumps orchitis
Photos: diffuse erythema of streptococcal toxic shock (A), purpura of meningococcal sepsis (B), shingles (C), erythema nodosum (D)
Common infections presenting with fever, grouped by site, with images (HSV encephalitis MRI, TB chest X-ray, empyema, cellulitis, liver and diverticular abscess, tibial TB osteomyelitis)
Body map of the usual organisms at each site, e.g. right-sided endocarditis from Staph. aureus in people who inject drugs; Kingella in joints of children 5 or under

sections.title: Pyrexia of unknown origin: definition, causes and focused assessment

blocks.text: **Davidson's definition of PUO:** temperature **above 38.0°C on several occasions for more than 3 weeks**, still undiagnosed after **1 week of investigation in hospital**. The time frame has since been loosened, so a work-up of 1 week of intensive ambulatory testing, three clinic visits or 3 inpatient days now counts. Subsets are HIV-related, immune-deficient and nosocomial PUO. **Up to one-third** of cases are never diagnosed.

The books differ. Talley defines PUO more loosely: documented fever above 38°C for more than 3 weeks with no cause after basic investigations. The series Talley quotes leaves only **10%** undiagnosed, while Davidson says **up to one-third**. Use Davidson's definition and figure in the exam.

blocks.title: Causes of PUO (series quoted by Talley)
rows: TB, occult abscess (usually abdominal or pelvic), osteomyelitis, infective endocarditis, brucellosis, CMV/EBV, HIV, malaria
Lymphoma, leukaemia; renal, hepatic or disseminated cancer; atrial myxoma
Systemic-onset juvenile RA / adult Still's disease, SLE, giant cell arteritis, polyarteritis nodosa
**Drug fever** (anticonvulsants, minocycline, allopurinol, heparin), IBD, sarcoidosis, multiple PEs, thyroiditis, haematoma, factitious fever

blocks.title: Principles
items: The longer the fever has lasted, the **less likely** it is to be infective
Most patients have a **common disease presenting unusually**, not a rare disease; a careful history can give the answer where costly tests have failed
Drug fever causes about **10%** of fevers that lead to hospital admission
A family history should prompt thoughts of periodic fever syndromes

blocks.title: Focused PUO history: go system by system
items: **GI:** diarrhoea, abdominal pain, recent abdominal surgery (IBD, diverticular disease, cholangitis)
**Cardiovascular:** known murmur or recent dental work (endocarditis); chest pain (pericarditis)
**Rheumatological:** joint symptoms, rashes, **persistent back pain** (spondylodiscitis)
**Neurological:** headache (meningitis, brain abscess)
**Genitourinary:** renal disease, past infection, dysuria
**Respiratory:** previous TB or TB contact, chest symptoms
Then travel, hobbies, pets, occupation, full drug history and HIV risk behaviour

blocks.title: Focused PUO examination (Talley)
rows: Choroidal tubercles / Roth's spots / retinal haemorrhages or infiltrates
Miliary TB / endocarditis / leukaemia or lymphoma
Dental abscess, tonsillar infection, otitis media, parotitis
Lymphoma, other malignancy, sarcoidosis, focal infection
Rose spots; hepatomegaly, ascites; **splenomegaly**; local tenderness
Typhoid; liver disease or SBP; haematological malignancy, endocarditis or malaria; pus collection
Testicular mass; rectal or pelvic mass or tenderness; pelvic pus
Seminoma or TB; pelvic abscess, carcinoma, prostatitis; PID
Chronic TB or cryptococcal meningitis; brain abscess, mononeuritis multiplex of PAN

blocks.title: Pattern recognition for unexplained fever (Talley)
items: Prosthetic heart valve → infective endocarditis
Young woman with a rash → SLE
Post-neurosurgery and on phenytoin → drug fever
Tired, middle-aged patient who bruises easily → blood cancer (leukaemia or lymphoma)
Recent young migrant from Nepal → tuberculosis

blocks.text: In PUO, **repeat the history and examination at intervals** to catch new signs (a rash, endocarditis stigmata, vasculitis). In men, consider the prostate as a hidden source, and keep **factitious fever** in mind.
Persistent back pain in PUO may be **spondylodiscitis**, which can progress to quadriplegia. Examine the spine for focal tenderness.

sections.title: HIV: risk history and examination signs

blocks.title: When to think of HIV
items: High-risk groups: men who have sex with men, people who inject drugs, sexual partners of people with HIV, people with haemophilia or who received blood products, sex workers and their contacts
**Test for HIV in any unexplained infectious illness**: Talley calls HIV the new great imitator
Suspect **HIV in anyone with TB**, and **TB in anyone with HIV** and a chronic respiratory illness

Chronic HIV features to ask about: fevers, night sweats, lymphadenopathy, fatigue, weight loss, chronic diarrhoea, seborrhoeic dermatitis, psoriasis, fungal infections, aphthous ulcers, neuropathy, cytopenias, kidney disease

blocks.title: HIV seroconversion illness (occurs in about half of cases)
History in a patient known to have HIV
items: Ask how the diagnosis was made, about a seroconversion illness, previous chest and other infections, hepatitis testing, treatment and the partner's awareness
If the patient is reluctant, questions about the **mode of infection can wait** for a later consultation, but they matter for public health
In treated HIV, **cardiovascular disease is now the commonest cause of death** (chronic inflammation plus metabolic effects of antiretrovirals), so ask about smoking, diabetes and hypertension

blocks.title: Examination signs in HIV
rows: 5–10 mm maculopapular rash on face and trunk
Herpes zoster, possibly over **more than one dermatome**
More often early than late HIV
Angry red vascular nodule that mimics Kaposi's
Painless white, often hairy-looking lesion on the **lateral border**
Oral hairy leucoplakia: EBV-driven, **almost diagnostic of HIV**
Soft exudates / old chorioretinal scar / perivascular haemorrhages + fluffy exudates
Common in AIDS / toxoplasmosis / **CMV retinitis** (rapid blindness)

blocks.text: A clear chest on auscultation does not exclude pneumonia in HIV: in **Pneumocystis jirovecii** and other opportunistic pneumonias the chest is often silent while the CXR shows infiltrates.

blocks.note: Bacillary angiomatosis (an angry red nodule) beside late Kaposi's sarcoma nodules: learn to tell these apart
Oral candidiasis plaques; Kaposi's sarcoma in the mouth and on the foot
Fundoscopy: old toxoplasma chorioretinal scar versus CMV retinitis with haemorrhages and fluffy exudates

sections.title: The acutely unwell, the returning traveller and vulnerable hosts

blocks.title: Kumar's three steps in fever or suspected sepsis
items: **Physiological assessment:** how sick is the patient? (observations, at presentation and repeatedly)
**Diagnostic assessment:** history, examination and early tests to find the site and the likely organism
**Management assessment:** antimicrobials, IV fluids or oxygen, source control (e.g. draining an abscess), infection control and organ support

blocks.title: Sepsis: risk factors and bedside signs
items: **Risk factors to ask about:** age under 1 or over 75; COPD or diabetes; chemotherapy, immunosuppressants or steroids; recent surgery, trauma or burns; pregnancy or the peripartum period; indwelling catheters or central lines
**NEWS** (UK) tracks temperature, heart rate, respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, blood pressure and consciousness
**Tachypnoea** is often the first sign; also look for a source (cellulitis, wound discharge, cough, dysuria), a **non-blanching rash**, low urine output, mottled skin, cyanosis and new AF
Elderly patients may present only with confusion, drowsiness or being 'off their legs'
Zero to Finals: assess and start treatment **within 1 hour** (Sepsis Six: 3 tests = lactate, blood cultures, urine output); oxygen target 94–98% (88–92% in COPD)

blocks.title: Sepsis and SIRS: which definition?
rows: Suspected infection + ≥2 of: SBP <100 mmHg, GCS ≤14, RR ≥22/min (or a SOFA rise of ≥2)
Sepsis where, after fluids, **vasopressors are needed to keep MAP >65 mmHg AND lactate is >2 mmol/L**
Zero to Finals: SBP <90 despite fluids, or lactate >4 mmol/L; also uses the older term 'severe sepsis' (organ dysfunction, lactate >2)
≥2 of: temperature >38.3°C or <36°C, HR >90, RR >20, raised WCC. Not specific: also follows burns, surgery, pancreatitis, thromboembolism

blocks.text: Definitions conflict: Zero to Finals still uses 'severe sepsis' and a septic shock threshold of SBP <90 or lactate >4. Davidson's 24e uses Sepsis-3 (vasopressors for MAP >65 **plus** lactate >2 after fluids). Note too that the SIRS fever cut-off is >38.3°C, while fever itself is defined as >38.0°C. Answer with Davidson's numbers.
Neutropenic or immunosuppressed patients can have **normal observations and temperature** while critically ill.

blocks.title: The returning traveller
items: WHO: fever from **1 week after entering a malaria area until 3 months after leaving** is a medical emergency

A malaria test (rapid antigen test plus thick and thin films) is **mandatory** in anyone unwell after being in a malarious area; Davidson repeats films on 3 consecutive days or uses a rapid diagnostic test
Common causes from low- and middle-income countries: malaria, typhoid, leptospirosis, dengue, chikungunya, dysentery, hepatitis A, amoebiasis, schistosomiasis, TB, tick typhus
Check a reliable travel-health source for current outbreaks in the countries visited

blocks.title: Fever in old age (Davidson)
items: Oral temperatures are **unreliable**: rectal or eardrum (tympanic) readings may be needed
Delirium with fever is common, especially with cerebrovascular disease or dementia
PUO causes: TB, intra-abdominal abscess, complicated UTI, endocarditis, polymyalgia rheumatica/temporal arteritis, tumours; fewer cases stay undiagnosed than in the young
Stroke and thromboembolism can cause fever, but look hard for a co-existing infection

blocks.title: First-line tests when fever has no obvious source
rows: FBC with differential **including eosinophils**, U&E, LFTs, glucose, muscle enzymes, ESR and CRP, HIV antibody, autoantibodies including ANA
CXR, ECG, urinalysis and urine culture, blood cultures, throat swab; malaria films, dengue NS1 and _S._ Typhi cultures where exposure is likely
Blood cultures ×2 (**×3 if endocarditis** or a deep infection is suspected); lactate and clotting if septic; sputum ×3 if TB is suspected
Only a **negative** dipstick for leucocytes and nitrites is useful

blocks.note: Algorithm for fever of unclear cause without sepsis: risk factors and exposures, symptom and medical history, examination checklist, tests, then differential and management

cards.front: Davidson: when can you call it fever?
cards.back: Only when a core temperature **above 38.0°C** has been recorded. Feeling hot or sweaty is not enough.

cards.front: What does a rigor mean, and why is it a red flag?
cards.back: A rapid rise in temperature from any cause; Talley: shaking chills suggest **bacteraemia**.

cards.front: Causes of sweating without a raised temperature?
cards.back: Alcohol, anxiety, thyrotoxicosis, diabetes, acromegaly, lymphoma, a hot environment.

cards.front: Kumar's four headings for an infection history?
cards.back: Patient, place, time, symptoms: why this patient, from here, now, with these symptoms?

cards.front: New vesicular rash: over what period do you ask about chickenpox or shingles contact?
cards.back: The previous **21 days** (the upper limit of the incubation period).

cards.front: Which GI infections do PPIs and H2 blockers predispose to?
cards.back: _Salmonella_ and _C. difficile_, but **not norovirus** (it is acid-insensitive).

cards.front: Kumar: which fever-plus-murmur combination suggests endocarditis?
cards.back: Temperature ≥37.8°C with a **new regurgitant systolic murmur**.

cards.front: New fever in an inpatient with a peripheral cannula?
cards.back: Remove the cannula and send the tip for culture.

cards.front: Red, hot, swollen limb: when do you suspect necrotising fasciitis?
cards.back: Pain severe or out of proportion to the signs, rapid progression, an 'odd' appearance.

Temperature >38.0°C on several occasions for >3 weeks, undiagnosed after 1 week of inpatient investigation (now relaxed to 3 inpatient days, 3 outpatient visits or 1 week of intensive ambulatory work-up).
Infection 30%, neoplasm 30%, connective tissue disease 15%, miscellaneous 15%, unknown 10%. Davidson: up to one-third stay undiagnosed.

cards.front: Typhoid rose spots: what do they look like and where?
cards.back: 2–4 mm flat red spots that blanch, on the upper abdomen and lower chest.

cards.front: Oral hairy leucoplakia: site, cause, significance?
cards.back: Painless white lesion on the lateral tongue, caused by EBV, almost diagnostic of HIV.

cards.front: At what CD4 count do oral and flexural candidiasis appear?
WHO time window for a malaria-risk fever in a traveller?
cards.back: From 1 week after entering a malaria area until 3 months after leaving: a medical emergency.
Sepsis needing vasopressors to keep MAP >65 mmHg **and** lactate >2 mmol/L despite fluid resuscitation.

cards.front: Fever in old age: how should you measure temperature?
cards.back: Oral readings are unreliable; use rectal or tympanic (eardrum) measurement.

questions.stem: A 47-year-old woman says she has felt hot and sweaty for 3 weeks, mostly at night. She has never measured her temperature. In clinic her temperature is 37.1°C and examination is normal.
questions.leadIn: Before she is labelled as having fever, what is required?
options: A subjective feeling of heat on at least two nights
questions.explanation: Davidson diagnoses fever only when a temperature **above 38.0°C is actually recorded**. Feeling hot or sweaty is not proof, and outpatients can be taught to keep a temperature chart.
whyNot: Subjective heat is exactly what Davidson says does not prove fever.
Axillary readings are less accurate than oral or rectal ones, and 37.5°C is below the threshold.
CRP shows inflammation but does not define fever.
Rigors reflect a fast rise in temperature, but fever still has to be measured.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man has had shivers for 3 days, a cough with green sputum and sharp right-sided chest pain on breathing in. He has not travelled.
questions.leadIn: Which organism is most likely?
questions.explanation: Kumar's time-course rule: a **short, acute history** points to organisms that cause acute disease. Three days of shivers, purulent sputum and pleuritic pain is the classic pneumococcal picture. A history longer than 2 weeks would push you towards TB, brucellosis, leishmaniasis or HIV.
whyNot: TB gives weeks to months of sweats, weight loss and cough, not a 3-day illness.
Brucellosis is a chronic febrile illness lasting more than 2 weeks.
Leishmaniasis is chronic and travel-related; he has not travelled.
HIV causes chronic illness or a seroconversion syndrome, not acute lobar pneumonia over 3 days.

questions.theme: Exposure history and the infection it suggests
questions.leadIn: For each patient, choose the most likely infection from the list. Any option can be the answer for one patient, several patients or none.

items.stem: A 29-year-old man canoes every weekend on rivers in northern England. Ten days after capsizing he develops fever, severe muscle aches and headache.
items.explanation: River water sports in a non-tropical country point to **leptospirosis**; Davidson's example is canoeists and windsurfers. Schistosomiasis needs freshwater exposure in endemic regions.

items.stem: A 52-year-old sheep farmer develops fever, headache and a dry cough during the lambing season.
items.explanation: Kumar links sheep contact with _Coxiella burnetii_, the cause of **Q fever**.

items.stem: A 31-year-old woman, 28 weeks pregnant, has fever and myalgia. Last week she ate a lot of soft unpasteurised cheese.
items.explanation: Two clues together: pregnancy increases susceptibility to listeriosis, and soft cheese is the classic source of _Listeria_.

items.stem: A 40-year-old man has a fever every other day. He has not left the UK this year, but 9 months ago he was treated for malaria after a trip to India.
items.explanation: Two-step inference: no recent travel, but **earlier travel** matters because some infections relapse. _P. vivax_ can recur months after the original illness.

questions.theme: Examination findings in the febrile patient
questions.leadIn: For each patient, choose the most likely diagnosis from the list. Any option can be the answer for one patient, several patients or none.

items.stem: A 36-year-old man who injects drugs has a temperature of 37.9°C, splinter haemorrhages and a new regurgitant systolic murmur.
items.explanation: Kumar: temperature ≥37.8°C with a **new regurgitant systolic murmur** suggests endocarditis; splinter haemorrhages and injecting drug use add weight.

items.stem: A 61-year-old man with diabetes has a red, swollen thigh. He is in severe pain that seems far worse than the skin changes, and the redness has spread a hand's breadth in 3 hours.
items.explanation: Pain out of proportion to the signs and rapid spread are Kumar's warning features for **necrotising fasciitis** rather than simple cellulitis.

items.stem: A 74-year-old woman develops a temperature of 38.6°C on day 4 after a hip replacement. Her wound is clean, but the skin around a forearm cannula is red and tender with a bead of pus.
items.explanation: New fever in an inpatient: look at device sites. Talley: remove the peripheral cannula and send the tip for culture.

items.stem: A 57-year-old man has had fever for 2 weeks and now has severe thoracic back pain. There is sharp tenderness when one vertebral spinous process is pressed.
items.explanation: Focal spinal tenderness in a febrile patient suggests **epidural abscess or discitis** (Davidson's musculoskeletal check).

questions.stem: A 71-year-old woman has had evening fevers to 38.4°C for 5 weeks, with weight loss and aching shoulders. She complains that brushing her hair hurts her scalp. Blood cultures, urine culture and chest X-ray were normal.
questions.leadIn: Which examination step is most likely to give the diagnosis?
options: Rectal examination for a pelvic mass
Palpation of the thyroid for tenderness
Inspection of the upper abdomen for rose spots
questions.explanation: In PUO, Talley's head and neck exam starts with the temporal arteries: **tender, thickened arteries** suggest giant cell arteritis. Scalp tenderness, shoulder aching and older age fit, and Davidson lists polymyalgia rheumatica/temporal arteritis as a prominent PUO cause in old age.
whyNot: Rectal examination looks for a pelvic abscess or carcinoma; nothing points there.
Choroidal tubercles suggest miliary TB, which does not explain scalp tenderness.
Thyroid tenderness suggests subacute thyroiditis; she has no neck symptoms.
Rose spots point to typhoid, which would not run for 5 weeks with scalp pain.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old man has had temperatures between 38.4°C and 38.9°C on many occasions over 4 weeks. His GP's blood tests have not found a cause.
questions.leadIn: Under Davidson's classic definition, what else is needed to call this pyrexia of unknown origin?
options: No diagnosis after 1 week of inpatient investigation
Three negative sets of blood cultures
A temperature above 39.0°C on at least one occasion
questions.explanation: Davidson's classic PUO: fever **>38.0°C** on several occasions for **more than 3 weeks**, undiagnosed after **1 week of investigation in hospital**. This has since been relaxed to 3 inpatient days, three outpatient visits or 1 week of intensive ambulatory work-up.
whyNot: SIRS describes a systemic inflammatory state, not PUO.
Negative cultures may be part of the work-up but are not the defining criterion.
Weight loss is a useful clue but not part of the definition.
The threshold is above 38.0°C; no higher peak is required.

questions.theme: Mucocutaneous and eye signs in HIV
questions.leadIn: For each patient, choose the most likely diagnosis from the list. Any option can be the answer for one patient, several patients or none.

items.stem: A 33-year-old man with HIV has a painless white lesion with a ridged, hair-like surface along the side of his tongue.
items.explanation: A painless white lesion on the **lateral tongue** is hairy leucoplakia, caused by EBV and almost diagnostic of HIV.

items.stem: A 45-year-old man with advanced HIV has several raised red-purple, non-tender lesions on the sole of his foot and a similar patch on his hard palate.
items.explanation: Red-purple, non-tender vascular tumours on skin and palate are **Kaposi's sarcoma**.

items.stem: A 39-year-old woman with a CD4 count of 30/mm³ notices her vision worsening over a few days. Fundoscopy shows haemorrhages along the vessels with fluffy white exudates.
items.explanation: Perivascular haemorrhages with fluffy exudates are **CMV retinitis**, which can cause blindness quickly.

items.stem: A 28-year-old man with HIV, who has a new kitten, has a bright red vascular nodule on his arm. It looks like Kaposi's sarcoma, but a biopsy grows a Bartonella species.
items.explanation: Two-step: a Kaposi-like vascular lesion caused by _Bartonella_ is **bacillary angiomatosis**, Kaposi's main mimic.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old man came back from Ghana 5 weeks ago. He has had fever, headache and watery diarrhoea for 2 days. He did not take malaria prophylaxis. His neck is supple.
questions.leadIn: What is the most important immediate investigation?
options: Malaria rapid antigen test with thick and thin blood films
questions.explanation: He is within the WHO window (1 week after entering to 3 months after leaving a malaria area), so this is an emergency and malaria testing is **mandatory**. Davidson warns that headache and diarrhoea occur in malaria without any CNS or gut infection, so do not be misled by them.
whyNot: Diarrhoea is a non-specific feature of malaria; stool tests can wait.
Headache without meningism is not a reason for LP before malaria is excluded.
Imaging does nothing for the likeliest, treatable diagnosis.
Hepatitis A is on the traveller list, but excluding malaria comes first.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old woman with pneumonia has received 30 mL/kg of IV fluid. Her blood pressure is still low, and she needs noradrenaline to keep her mean arterial pressure at 66 mmHg. Her lactate is 3.1 mmol/L.
questions.leadIn: Under Davidson's definitions, what is her condition?
questions.explanation: Davidson (Sepsis-3): **septic shock** = sepsis in which, after fluid resuscitation, vasopressors are needed to keep **MAP >65 mmHg** and lactate is **>2 mmol/L**. She meets both.
whyNot: Needing a vasopressor with a raised lactate moves her beyond sepsis alone.
'Severe sepsis' is an older term (still used by Zero to Finals) that Sepsis-3 dropped.
She has a clear infection (pneumonia), so SIRS without infection does not fit.
Bacteraemia describes bacteria in the blood, not her physiological state.

questions.leadIn: For each patient, choose the most likely diagnosis from the list. Any option can be the answer for one patient, several patients or none.

items.stem: A 23-year-old man has had a fever of 39.5°C for a week after visiting relatives in Pakistan. He is constipated, his pulse is 72/min, and there are a few 3 mm blanching pink spots on his upper abdomen.
items.explanation: Fever, constipation, rose spots on the upper abdomen and a pulse slower than expected for the fever (relative bradycardia) is the typhoid pattern.

items.stem: A 19-year-old student has a sore throat, fever and enlarged neck nodes. Two days after starting ampicillin she develops a widespread rash.
items.explanation: A rash after ampicillin in a young patient with pharyngitis and lymphadenopathy is the keyword pattern for **infectious mononucleosis**.

items.stem: A 42-year-old man has fever, right upper quadrant pain and a tender enlarged liver, with crackles at the right lung base. He had bloody diarrhoea in India 3 months ago.
items.explanation: Fever + tender hepatomegaly + basal crackles, after dysentery abroad, fits an **amoebic liver abscess**.

items.stem: A 30-year-old woman develops fever and aches 6 days after returning from Thailand. The fever settles for 2 days, then returns with a rash.
items.explanation: Two-step: tropical travel plus a **biphasic** fever pattern points to dengue (Kumar's example of a characteristic time course).

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman has her third skin abscess in 6 months. Her partner and her teenage son have had similar boils.
questions.leadIn: Which organism is the main concern?
questions.explanation: Kumar: a patient with **recurrent skin abscesses** is asked about contacts with similar infections because of the risk of spreading **PVL-producing _Staph. aureus_**.
whyNot: Group A strep causes cellulitis and impetigo rather than recurrent boils clustered in a household.
Pseudomonas is not the organism Kumar links to recurrent household boils.
Candida does not cause recurrent cutaneous abscesses in healthy people.
Nocardia is an opportunist in the immunosuppressed, not a household boil organism.

questions.stem: A 44-year-old man had his spleen removed after a road traffic accident. He now has a high fever and feels very unwell.
questions.leadIn: Which organism is he most at risk from?
questions.explanation: Without a spleen, patients are vulnerable to **capsulated bacteria**: pneumococcus, _Haemophilus_ and meningococcus.
whyNot: Pneumocystis is a problem of T-cell immunosuppression such as HIV, not asplenia.
CMV affects transplant and HIV patients, not asplenic patients specifically.
Candida infection follows neutropenia, lines or antibiotics, not splenectomy.
MAC affects advanced HIV.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old man has fever, a sore throat, enlarged neck nodes, aching joints and a rash of 5–10 mm pink macules and papules on his face and trunk. He has had no antibiotics. A heterophile antibody (Paul–Bunnell) test is negative. He began a new sexual relationship 4 weeks ago.
questions.leadIn: Which test is most important not to omit?
options: Repeat heterophile antibody test in a week
questions.explanation: This is the picture of **HIV seroconversion**: fever, lymphadenopathy, pharyngitis, a maculopapular rash on face and trunk and arthralgia. Kumar includes HIV among the glandular fever syndromes, and Talley says to test for HIV in any unexplained infectious illness.
whyNot: ASO supports recent strep infection but would not explain the rash and risk history.
Repeating the EBV test delays the diagnosis that matters.
A throat swab looks for streptococcal tonsillitis but misses the key diagnosis.
Atypical lymphocytes occur in several viral infections and are not specific.

questions.stem: An 84-year-old woman in a nursing home has become newly confused and is eating poorly. Her oral temperature is 37.2°C and her respiratory rate is 24/min.
questions.leadIn: What is the best way to establish whether she has a fever?
options: Measure a rectal or tympanic temperature
Repeat the oral temperature in 4 hours
Ask her whether she feels hot
Use the CRP as a substitute for temperature
questions.explanation: Davidson: in old age **oral temperatures are unreliable**, so fever may be missed; rectal or eardrum (tympanic) measurement may be needed. (Davidson's general history box rates ear readings below oral or rectal ones, but its old-age box endorses eardrum reflectance for core temperature, so rectal or tympanic is the answer here.) New confusion and tachypnoea in an older person should prompt a search for infection.
whyNot: Axillary readings are less accurate than oral ones, never more.
Repeating an unreliable method does not solve the problem.
Feeling hot does not prove fever, and she is confused.
CRP shows inflammation but does not measure temperature.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with a mechanical aortic valve has felt unwell for 2 months, with evening sweats and fevers up to 38.5°C. He had a dental extraction 3 months ago. He has lost 4 kg.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: **Step 1: define the problem.** More than 3 weeks of documented fever above 38°C, so think in PUO terms. **Step 2: define the host.** Davidson's past history asks about prosthetic material, and he has a prosthetic valve. **Step 3: look for an exposure.** Talley's CVS review asks about dental procedures. **Step 4: pattern match.** Talley's scenario 'adult with a prosthetic valve' points straight to endocarditis. **Step 5: plan the exam.** Look for splinter haemorrhages, Janeway lesions, Roth's spots, a changed prosthetic sound or new murmur, and splenomegaly.
whyNot: TB is a major PUO cause, but nothing here (no cough, contact or migration) points to it ahead of the valve.
Lymphoma causes sweats and weight loss but ignores the valve and the dental trigger.
Drug fever needs a culprit drug; none is mentioned.
PMR causes PUO in older people but not with a prosthetic valve and a dental trigger.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman complains of drenching night sweats, weight loss despite a good appetite, palpitations and a fine tremor. Four temperatures recorded at home and in clinic were all between 36.6°C and 37.2°C. She has no lymphadenopathy.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely cause of her sweating?
questions.explanation: **Step 1: is there fever?** No: fever needs a recorded temperature >38.0°C, and she has repeated normal readings. **Step 2: use the list of sweating without fever.** Davidson's list includes alcohol, anxiety, **thyrotoxicosis**, diabetes, acromegaly, lymphoma and heat. **Step 3: pick the discriminators.** Weight loss despite a good appetite, palpitations and tremor fit thyrotoxicosis; no lymphadenopathy makes lymphoma less likely.
whyNot: TB causes night sweats with documented fever; her temperature is repeatedly normal.
Endocarditis is a febrile illness, and she has no fever and no murmur.
Lymphoma can cause sweats without fever, but tremor, palpitations and a good appetite fit thyroid better, and she has no nodes.
HIV gives fever and lymphadenopathy, not tremor and palpitations.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old man has had a dry cough and worsening breathlessness on exertion for 3 weeks. He has white plaques in his mouth and has lost weight. His chest sounds clear on auscultation, but a chest X-ray shows bilateral infiltrates.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: **Step 1: find the clue to the host.** Oral candidiasis appears once the CD4 count is below 200/mm³, so suspect advanced HIV. **Step 2: compare the exam with the X-ray.** Talley notes that in Pneumocystis and other opportunistic pneumonias the chest is often **clear despite infiltrates on CXR**. **Step 3: check the time course.** Three weeks of dry cough and exertional breathlessness is subacute, not the abrupt lobar picture. **Step 4: act.** Offer an HIV test (routine in unexplained infection).
whyNot: Pneumococcal pneumonia is acute with focal crackles and purulent sputum.
Kaposi's sarcoma can occur anywhere, but a clinically silent chest with infiltrates and candidiasis is the classic Pneumocystis picture.
Talley links bronchiolitis obliterans to basal crackles, not a clear chest.
A lung abscess gives purulent sputum and a focal cavity, not bilateral infiltrates.

questions.theme: Risk factors and the infections they predispose to
questions.leadIn: For each patient, choose the most likely infection from the list. Any option can be the answer for one patient, several patients or none.
options: Staphylococcus aureus bacteraemia with right-sided endocarditis

items.stem: A 33-year-old man injects heroin into his groin. He has fever, rigors and a pansystolic murmur at the lower left sternal edge.
items.explanation: Injecting drug use leads to _Staph. aureus_ bloodstream infection, and endocarditis in this group is often **right-sided**.

items.stem: A 55-year-old man with alcohol-related liver disease and tense ascites develops fever and diffuse abdominal tenderness.
items.explanation: Kumar: alcohol excess with ascites links to **spontaneous bacterial peritonitis**.

items.stem: A 64-year-old woman had hip surgery in a hospital abroad 3 weeks ago. She now has a urinary infection that has not responded to two standard antibiotics.
items.explanation: Hospital treatment abroad carries a risk of antibiotic-resistant bacteria; worldwide, multi-resistant Gram-negatives are a key concern.

items.stem: A 70-year-old man was recovering from influenza when he suddenly worsened, with high fever, hypotension and diffuse red skin.
items.explanation: Two-step: recent influenza predisposes to **secondary group A strep** infection, and diffuse erythema with shock is the streptococcal toxic shock picture.

questions.theme: Pyrexia of unknown origin: focused clinical clues
questions.leadIn: For each patient, choose the most likely diagnosis from the list. Any option can be the answer for one patient, several patients or none.

items.stem: A 47-year-old man has had fevers for 3 weeks after neurosurgery for a meningioma. He started phenytoin after the operation. His wound is clean, and cultures and imaging are unremarkable.
items.explanation: Talley's scenario: post-neurosurgery on phenytoin suggests **drug fever**; anticonvulsants are a classic cause.

items.stem: A 26-year-old woman has fever, painful joints and mouth ulcers. She has a red, butterfly-shaped rash on her face.
items.explanation: A butterfly rash in a young woman with fever points to **SLE**.

items.stem: A 39-year-old woman has had fever for 3 weeks, starting soon after a cold. Her neck is sore, and a tender, slightly enlarged thyroid is palpable.
items.explanation: Thyroid tenderness in PUO suggests **subacute thyroiditis** (Talley's neck examination).

items.stem: A 24-year-old man who moved from Nepal a year ago has had fever and weight loss for 5 weeks. Fundoscopy shows several small pale yellow lesions in the choroid.
items.explanation: Two-step: a young migrant from Nepal suggests TB, and **choroidal tubercles** on fundoscopy mean miliary spread.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old man with gout started allopurinol 2 weeks ago. He now has a daily fever of 38.5°C. Examination is normal, and blood cultures, urine culture and chest X-ray are negative.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely cause of his fever?
questions.explanation: Talley lists **allopurinol** among drug-fever culprits, with anticonvulsants, minocycline and heparin. Drug fever causes about 10% of fevers that lead to admission, which is why Davidson asks about drugs that can themselves cause fever.
whyNot: An abscess usually gives localising pain or tenderness, and there is a clear drug trigger here.
Endocarditis needs a predisposition or a murmur; neither is present.
TB gives a longer illness with weight loss and sweats.
Lymphoma is less likely than a drug started just before the fever.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old married woman has persistent oral thrush and has lost 6 kg. She has never injected drugs or had a blood transfusion and says she 'is not in a risk group'.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Defer HIV testing because she has no risk factors
Test for HIV only if her husband agrees
Treat the thrush and review in 3 months
questions.explanation: Davidson reminds you that the **commonest route of HIV-1 transmission is heterosexual**, so 'no risk group' does not exclude HIV. Talley: HIV testing should be routine in any unexplained infectious illness, and oral candidiasis suggests a low CD4 count.
whyNot: Most HIV is acquired heterosexually; not belonging to a classic risk group does not make her low-risk.
Her testing does not depend on her partner's consent.
Delaying 3 months risks missing advanced HIV.
A glucose check alone ignores the weight loss and persistent candidiasis, which call for an HIV test.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old primary school teacher develops a new vesicular rash and fever. You want to know whether she has been exposed to chickenpox or shingles.
questions.leadIn: Over what period before the rash should you ask about contacts?
questions.explanation: Kumar: a new vesicular rash prompts questions about chickenpox or shingles contact in the **previous 21 days**, the upper limit of the incubation period. An exposure further back than that is unlikely to be the cause. Teachers are exposed to common childhood infections.
whyNot: 3 days is far shorter than the incubation period of chickenpox.
7 days would miss most exposures, as the incubation period runs up to 21 days.
6 weeks is longer than the incubation period, so such exposures are unlikely to be relevant.
3 months is the WHO malaria window for travellers, not the chickenpox incubation period.

questions.leadIn: For each patient, choose the most likely site of infection from the list. Any option can be the answer for one patient, several patients or none.

items.stem: A 72-year-old woman has fever and left iliac fossa pain. There is tenderness with guarding in the left iliac fossa, and bowel sounds are reduced.
items.explanation: Localised left iliac fossa tenderness with guarding is Davidson's example of diverticulitis; Kumar links it to a diverticular abscess.

items.stem: A 24-year-old woman has fever, rigors, dysuria and pain in her right loin. Pressing over the right renal angle is very painful.
items.explanation: Renal angle tenderness with urinary symptoms points to **pyelonephritis**.

items.stem: A 67-year-old man has fever, perineal ache and pain on passing urine. Rectal examination finds a very tender prostate.
items.explanation: A tender prostate on rectal examination indicates **prostatitis**; in men the prostate is a hidden source of fever.

items.stem: A 52-year-old man has fever and right upper abdominal pain, but his abdomen is soft and not tender. There are bronchial breath sounds and crackles at the right lung base.
items.explanation: Two-step: abdominal pain with a normal abdomen but focal chest signs means a **basal pneumonia** referring pain to the abdomen, one of the pitfalls of localising symptoms.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man is admitted with acute pancreatitis due to gallstones. His temperature is 38.5°C, pulse 112/min, respiratory rate 24/min and white cell count 15 × 10⁹/L. No source of infection has been found yet.
questions.leadIn: Which term best describes his current state?
questions.explanation: He meets all four SIRS criteria (temperature >38.3°C, HR >90, RR >20, raised WCC). Talley stresses that SIRS is not specific to infection: it also follows pancreatitis, burns, surgery and thromboembolism, although sepsis must still be excluded.
whyNot: Septic shock needs proven or suspected infection with vasopressor-dependent hypotension and a raised lactate.
PUO needs more than 3 weeks of fever without a diagnosis.
Bacteraemia needs bacteria in the blood, which has not been shown.
His white cell count is high, not low.

questions.stem: Five patients present with a fever of 38.3°C.
questions.leadIn: Which patient is at greatest risk of an opportunistic infection?
options: A 76-year-old man with diabetes who had a liver transplant 2 months ago and takes two immunosuppressants
A 60-year-old woman on low-dose prednisolone for polymyalgia rheumatica
A 25-year-old woman who is 20 weeks pregnant
A 70-year-old woman who had a splenectomy 20 years ago
questions.explanation: Kumar asks you to judge the **net state of immunosuppression**: age, co-morbidity and drugs add up. The **first 6 months after solid organ transplant** is the most intense period, and transplant recipients are open to fungi, low-virulence viruses and non-tuberculous mycobacteria.
whyNot: Low-dose maintenance steroid alone is a much smaller risk than multiple anti-rejection drugs early after transplant.
Pregnancy raises the risk of specific infections (malaria, HIV, listeriosis) but is not a state of opportunistic infection risk like early transplant.
Treated hypertension does not impair immunity.
Asplenia predisposes to capsulated bacteria, not to opportunistic pathogens.

ospe.identify: Splinter haemorrhages (fine dark lines under the nails) and Roth's spots in the retina: think **infective endocarditis**
Diffuse erythema = streptococcal toxic shock; non-blanching purpura = **meningococcal sepsis** (an emergency)
Grouped vesicles in a dermatome = shingles; painful nodules on the shins = erythema nodosum (has non-infective causes too)
Imaging of febrile syndromes: temporal lobe enhancement on MRI = HSV encephalitis; CT collections = pyogenic liver or diverticular abscess
Angry red nodule = bacillary angiomatosis (Bartonella); red-purple non-tender nodules = **Kaposi's sarcoma**
White oral plaques = candidiasis (CD4 <200); purple palatal or foot lesions = Kaposi's sarcoma
Pigmented chorioretinal scar = old toxoplasmosis; haemorrhages with fluffy white exudates along vessels = **CMV retinitis**
